---
title: "Quiz: B-splines and NURBS"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does "a curve is a linear combination of basis functions" mean for a B-spline curve? What plays the role of the coefficients?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mathbf{C}(t) = \sum_i \mathbf{P}_i N_i(t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every curve point is a weighted sum of the control points, with weights given by fixed bump functions $N_i(t)$ of the parameter. The control points are the coefficients (the coordinates of the curve in the basis), one 2D coefficient per bump.
:::

---

**Q2.** Nearest-neighbour, linear and cubic B-spline interpolation correspond to B-splines of which degrees? Which of them pass through the data values when the data are used directly as control values?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at each bump's values at the integers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Degrees 0 (box), 1 (hat) and 3 (cubic bell). The box and the hat are 1 at their own sample and 0 at all others, so they interpolate. The cubic bell has values $\tfrac16, \tfrac46, \tfrac16$ at the integers: used directly, it averages neighbouring values and does **not** pass through them (it smooths). Unit 4 fixes this with a prefilter.
:::

---

**Q3.** A closed uniform cubic B-spline has control points $(0,0), (6,0), (6,6), (0,6)$. Where is the curve point at the knot that belongs to $(6, 0)$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Weights $\tfrac16, \tfrac46, \tfrac16$ on the point and its two neighbours.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\tfrac16[(0,0) + 4(6,0) + (6,6)] = \tfrac16(30, 6) = (5, 1)$: inside the square, the corner is cut.
:::

---

**Q4.** A cubic B-spline curve has 20 control points. You move control point 10. How many spans (knot intervals) of the curve change? What would change in a single Bézier curve of degree 19 through the same points?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Support of a cubic basis function.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
4 spans (the support of $N_{10,3}$ covers 4 knot intervals); the rest of the curve does not move. In the degree-19 Bézier curve every point except the two ends moves.
:::

---

**Q5.** What does a triple interior knot do to a cubic B-spline curve? Why might you want one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Continuity $C^{p - m}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The curve is only $C^{3-3} = C^0$ there: it passes through a control point and can have a sharp corner, while staying C² everywhere else. Useful for outlines with real corners (a crystal, a cut edge) in an otherwise smooth curve.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can no polynomial curve trace a circle exactly, and what do NURBS add to make it possible?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Rational functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A circle needs $x(t)^2 + y(t)^2 = 1$ for all $t$; polynomials cannot do this (other than constants), so polynomial circles are always approximations (the best cubic Bézier quarter circle is off by 0.027 %). NURBS give every control point a weight and divide by the weighted sum of the basis functions: rational functions, such as $x = (1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2)$, $y = 2t/(1 + t^2)$, can trace a circle exactly.
:::

---

**Q7.** In the NURBS mechanism "lift, evaluate, divide", what are the lifted coordinates of a control point $(3, -1)$ with weight 2, and what happens if all weights are equal?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$(w x, w y, w)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(6, -2, 2)$. If all weights equal $w$, the third coordinate of the evaluated point is $w\sum_i N_i = w$, and dividing by it gives back the ordinary B-spline curve: the weights only matter when they differ.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Use Cox–de Boor on the uniform knots $0, 1, 2, 3$ to compute $N_{0,2}(0.5)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At $t = 0.5$ only $N_{0,0}$ is non-zero among the boxes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$N_{0,0}(0.5) = 1$, $N_{1,0}(0.5) = 0$. $N_{0,1}(0.5) = \frac{0.5 - 0}{1 - 0}\cdot 1 + \frac{2 - 0.5}{2 - 1}\cdot 0 = 0.5$, $N_{1,1}(0.5) = 0$. $N_{0,2}(0.5) = \frac{0.5 - 0}{2 - 0}\cdot 0.5 + \frac{3 - 0.5}{3 - 1}\cdot 0 = 0.125$.
:::
